teaser: In 1917 a police officer ordered paintings like this out of a Paris shop window.
review_notes:
It is not certain that this exact canvas hung in the Berthe Weill show of December 3, 1917; lesson says 'nudes like this one'.
Story of the police commissioner objecting to body hair comes from Berthe Weill's memoirs.
Size 60.6 x 92.7 cm; Met credit: The Mr. and Mrs. Klaus G. Perls Collection, 1997.
Number of nudes in the series: 'roughly two dozen' (sources give 22 to about 30).
Zborowski arrangement (room in his apartment on rue Joseph-Bara, daily allowance, paid models) is standard but details vary.
2015 Christie's sale of another Nu couche for $170.4 million.
In the image one eye appears pale and blank, the other darker: check wording against the original.

lesson.text: Paris, December 3, 1917. A small crowd gathers on the sidewalk outside Berthe Weill's gallery, staring at the window. Inside hang several nudes like this one. Across the street is a police station. Before the evening is over, an officer has summoned the dealer and ordered the pictures taken down.

It was the only solo exhibition Amedeo Modigliani had in his lifetime, and it nearly closed on its first day. Almost nothing sold. The painter was 33, Italian, poor, already sick with tuberculosis, and known in Montparnasse more for his drinking than for his art.

What was so shocking? Paris museums were full of naked goddesses. But those came with an excuse: a myth, a cupid, a faraway setting. Modigliani gives no excuse. This is a modern woman on a couch, in a room, now.

According to Berthe Weill, the police officer's precise complaint was that the nudes had body hair. Polished academic nudes were painted hairless, like marble. Hair meant a real woman, and that was the offense.
In this canvas you can check that for yourself, and see how little else there is. The picture is about 61 by 93 cm (24 by 36.5 inches), and the body takes up nearly all of it.

lesson.title: A body that fills the frame
lesson.text: Three places where Modigliani breaks the polite rules of the nude.

spots.title: Underarm
spots.text: A few dark strokes of hair under the raised arm. Small, but exactly the kind of detail that made the police object.

spots.title: Arms cut off
spots.text: Her forearms and hands run out of the picture at the left edge. She is too close to fit, as if seen from the edge of the bed.

spots.title: Legs cut off
spots.text: At the right, the thighs are sliced by the frame. No feet, no hands: the painting keeps only the long middle of the body.

lesson.text: That cropping is why she feels so near. Older reclining nudes, like Titian's Venus of Urbino, lie fully inside their rooms with space to spare. Modigliani zooms in until the canvas can barely hold her, the way a photographer might.

He painted her because someone finally paid him to. His dealer, the Polish poet Léopold Zborowski, gave him a room in his own apartment, canvases, paint, models and a small daily allowance. Between 1916 and 1919 Modigliani produced roughly two dozen nudes there.
Modigliani took the oldest subject in European painting, the reclining nude, and removed the myth, the distance and the modesty.

Before these paintings, he had spent about five years carving stone heads, under the spell of the sculptor Brancusi and of African and ancient sculpture. Dust, cost and his weak lungs made him stop. But he kept thinking like a carver, and you can see it in the outline.
Trace the two edges of the body.

lines.label: Upper contour
lines.text: From shoulder to waist the line sinks, then swings up over the hip. One unbroken curve, like the edge of a carved stone.

lines.label: Lower contour
lines.text: Underneath, a thin dark line follows the back and thigh. Modigliani draws the body with a brush first, then fills it.

lines.label: The long axis
lines.text: The whole figure stretches corner to corner in a slow wave. Nothing interrupts it: no jewelry, no drapery, no shadow cast on the couch.

lesson.text: Inside those outlines the flesh is almost one color, a warm apricot, with very little shading. He sets it against deep reds and browns so that it glows. The body is not modeled like a statue in a museum. It is a flat, luminous shape with a sharp edge.
Modigliani was famous for speed. Friends recalled that he liked to finish a portrait in one or two sittings, and that he rarely went back to correct a canvas.
And the face? It belongs to the same family as his stone heads: long nose, small pursed mouth, almond eyes. Her head is turned toward you, tipped onto her arm. She knows she is being looked at.
Modigliani signed this canvas in paint, in a place where it almost disappears into the dark. Where?

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: Top right, in thin reddish letters on the dark wall: “modigliani”, lowercase. It sits as far from the body as the canvas allows.

lesson.text: The model's name is lost. Zborowski hired professional models, and Modigliani did not record them. That anonymity is part of the effect: she is not a goddess and not a portrait of somebody. She is simply present.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: A long nose drawn in one line, a small red mouth. One eye is pale and blank, the other darker, as if half asleep and half watching.

spots.title: White pillow
spots.text: Thick, chalky white behind her head. It is the brightest patch in the picture and pushes the dark hair forward.

spots.title: Barely shaded
spots.text: The chest is rounded by the outline alone, with only a faint change of tone. Compare that with the heavy shadows of older nudes.

spots.title: The patterned cover
spots.text: Loose pale curls suggest a printed or embroidered fabric. Modigliani hints at the pattern and moves on.

spots.title: The dark edge
spots.text: Here the outline of the hip is clearest: a thin, nearly black line between warm flesh and red cloth.

spots.title: White cloth
spots.text: A second patch of white at the lower right answers the pillow at upper left. The two whites pin down the diagonal of the body.

lesson.text: The pictures the police wanted hidden are now among the most expensive ever sold. In 2015 another reclining nude from the same series went for 170.4 million dollars at auction. This one came to the Metropolitan Museum as a gift in 1997.

quiz.question: What happened at Modigliani's only solo exhibition, in December 1917?
options: The police ordered nudes taken down
Every painting sold on the first night
quiz.explanation: An officer from the station across the street had the nudes removed.

quiz.question: According to the dealer Berthe Weill, what did the police object to?
quiz.explanation: Academic nudes were hairless; hair signaled a real, present woman.

quiz.question: Who made the series of nudes possible?
quiz.explanation: Zborowski supplied a room, materials, models and a daily allowance.

quiz.question: How does Modigliani make the woman feel so close?
options: He crops her arms and legs at the edges of the canvas
He paints her larger than life on a wall
quiz.explanation: Hands and feet run out of the frame, as in a close-up.

quiz.question: What did Modigliani do for about five years before these paintings?
quiz.explanation: He was a sculptor first, and his outlines still think like a carver's.

quiz.question: Where is the signature?
options: Bottom left, on the white cloth
In the center of the couch
Top right, on the dark wall
quiz.explanation: It is written in thin lowercase letters in the upper right corner.

facts.text: Modigliani had many successful solo exhibitions during his life.
facts.explanation: He had only one, in 1917, and almost nothing sold.

facts.text: The model's hands and feet are not visible in the painting.
facts.explanation: The frame cuts her arms at the left and her legs at the right.

facts.text: The flesh is built up with deep shadows, like a marble statue under a spotlight.
facts.explanation: The body is almost one warm color, shaped mainly by its outline.
